a.summary: MIGRATION.md tells implementors the deprecation costs them nothing, but the deprecated `sign(SequencedCollection)` is abstract, so every implementation is warned now and must be renamed at removal.
a.failure_scenario:
MIGRATION.md:105-107 reads "The existing single-signer, explicit-index, and `Collection<Signer>` overloads remain undeprecated. Named positional aliases delegate to the corresponding existing overload, including custom convenience overrides. New instance methods have defaults, so existing `Transaction` implementations do not need additional method overrides." A maintainer of a third-party `Transaction` reads this, concludes the release is a no-op for them, and upgrades. Their build then emits (or, under `-Werror`, fails on) `[removal] sign(SequencedCollection<Signer>) in Transaction has been deprecated and marked for removal` at their own `@Override` — not at any call site they can change. Nothing in the section states that the deprecated `SequencedCollection` overload at Transaction.java:784 is abstract, that implementing it is itself a flagged use, or that at removal they must rename the override to `signInOrder`. The sentence is literally about the NEW methods and is true of them, which is what makes it misleading: the whole implementor-side cost of the change is the one thing the section does not mention.
AGENTS.md:69 requires the deprecation to say "what changed and how to keep the old behaviour"; for an implementor (as opposed to a caller) no such path is stated anywhere.

b.summary: "New instance methods have defaults, so existing Transaction implementations do not need additional method overrides" is true only of the new methods, and the section never tells implementors that the one abstract member in the deprecated set is itself marked for removal.
b.failure_scenario: A third-party `Transaction` implementor reads this section, sees the closing sentence, and concludes there is nothing for them to do. But `void sign(SequencedCollection<Signer> signers)` at Transaction.java:783-784 is abstract AND `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` — the only abstract member in the deprecated set — so they must keep implementing a for-removal method, and javac issues no deprecation warning for merely overriding one, so they get no signal. At removal, `signInOrder(SequencedCollection)` (Transaction.java:845-847), which today is a default that delegates to that abstract method, has to become abstract itself — requiring from that implementor exactly the "additional method override" this sentence says is unnecessary. The audience with actual work to do is the one the section reassures.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.

claims_new_evidence.instructions: Does `b` cite evidence that `a` does not?

criteria.true: `b` names a file, test, command, observation, or reproduction that `a` does not mention.
criteria.false: `b` cites nothing beyond what `a` already cites, or cites nothing at all.
